items.title: Famine in 1944 affected the grandchildren of survivors
items.claim: The Dutch Hongerwinter (1944-1945) caused severe famine for several months. Decades later, the GRANDchildren of women pregnant during the famine showed altered methylation patterns and different rates of metabolic disease — even though they were never themselves underfed.
items.prompt: How does an environmental stress affect three generations?

options.text: Epigenetic marks (especially DNA methylation patterns) acquired during fetal development can persist into adulthood; some can affect germline cells, allowing the next generation to inherit the modified pattern
It must be a DNA sequence mutation caused by famine
Famine alters social behaviour passed to grandchildren culturally

items.reveal_title: Heijmans, Tobi and colleagues — the Hongerwinter epigenetic study
items.reveal:
Heijmans et al. (2008) compared DNA methylation in adults who had been in utero during the Dutch famine to their unexposed siblings. The famine-exposed showed less methylation at the IGF2 gene 60 years later.

More recent work has shown some methylation marks pass to grandchildren, with associated health correlates.

This is not classical Lamarckism (inheritance of acquired characteristics through soft inheritance). Methylation marks are mostly cleared between generations, but some escape erasure. The mechanisms are still being mapped.

Distinguishing real intergenerational inheritance from confounders (in utero exposure, shared environment) requires careful study design. Animal models (rodents) have been used to confirm causal mechanisms.
items.why: Inheritance is taught as DNA sequence transmission. Some heritable information is encoded above the sequence, in modifications to DNA and chromatin — and famine can leave its mark across decades.

items.title: The most abundant enzyme on Earth is bad at its job
items.claim: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide into sugar in every photosynthesising organism. It's the most abundant protein on the planet (about half a kilogram in every square metre of leaf). It's also slow (3 reactions per second per active site) and confuses CO2 with O2.
items.prompt: Why do plants invest so heavily in such a flawed enzyme?

options.text: There's no alternative — Rubisco is the only carbon-fixation enzyme that works

Rubisco evolved when the atmosphere had little O2; the confusion between CO2 and O2 was rare then. Now plants mass-produce it (often 50 percent of leaf protein) to compensate for its slowness, and C4 plants concentrate CO2 around it to outcompete O2 binding
Rubisco is highly efficient — the textbook is wrong

items.reveal:
Rubisco's active site binds CO2 by inserting it into a bound substrate (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate). About 25 percent of the time at room temperature, it grabs O2 instead — initiating photorespiration, a wasteful cycle that costs energy and releases CO2.

This was tolerable in the Proterozoic atmosphere (low O2, high CO2). As oxygen rose and CO2 dropped, the problem grew.

C4 plants (corn, sugarcane) evolved an extra carbon-fixation step in mesophyll cells (using PEP carboxylase, which doesn't confuse O2). This shuttles CO2 into specialised bundle-sheath cells at high concentration, where Rubisco then operates without interference.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapples) do the same trick temporally — fixing CO2 at night when stomata can be open without losing water.
items.why: Evolution doesn't engineer optimal enzymes — it tinkers around constraints inherited from earlier conditions. Rubisco is a beautiful example of a molecular legacy system.

items.title: Sea otters maintain entire underwater forests
items.claim: Where sea otters live, kelp forests thrive. Where they have been hunted to near-extinction, sea urchins explode and graze kelp to bare rock ('urchin barrens'). One otter eats about 25% of its body mass in urchins daily.
items.prompt: What makes otters a keystone species?

options.text: They are the largest predators present
They selectively eat sea urchins, the only major kelp grazer in the system; removing otters releases urchin populations, which devastate kelp forests that support hundreds of other species
Otters fertilise the water with their waste

items.reveal:
Jim Estes and John Palmisano (1974) compared Aleutian islands with otters to islands where otters had been wiped out for the fur trade. The contrast was startling: lush kelp forests vs barren urchin-grazed rock.

Kelp forests are enormously productive. They support fish, invertebrates, sea birds, marine mammals. They sequester carbon. They dampen wave energy and protect coasts.

Subsequent work (Estes et al. 1998) suggested that killer whale predation on sea otters — possibly because their normal prey, large whales, had been depleted by whaling — was driving a SECOND collapse of Aleutian otter populations, with knock-on collapses of kelp.

A whaling-era extinction cascade may still be propagating decades later. Ecosystems have memory.

The 'keystone species' concept (Paine 1969) was based on starfish; otters became its most famous illustration. Many ecosystems have keystones; identifying them before they collapse is a recurring conservation challenge.
items.why: Big effects from one species seem improbable. In sea otter ecosystems, the entire architecture depends on one mid-sized predator preventing one herbivore from grazing the forest down.
